questions.question: How does MySQL primary-replica replication work and how does it affect a Spring Boot application's read/write strategy?
questions.title: MySQL Replication: Primary-Replica Setup
questions.direct_answer: MySQL replication streams **binary log (binlog)** events from the primary to one or more replicas asynchronously. On each replica an **I/O thread** pulls binlog events into a local relay log, and an **SQL thread** (or multi-threaded workers) replays them. In Spring Boot, you configure separate DataSource beans for writes (primary) and reads (replicas) and use `AbstractRoutingDataSource` with `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` to split traffic, while handling replication lag for read-your-writes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the full replication pipeline (binlog, I/O thread, relay log, SQL thread), the consistency trade-offs of async vs semi-sync, and how to implement read/write splitting in a Spring Boot application.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Routing reads to replicas without considering replication lag, producing read-your-writes bugs where users do not see their own changes. Another common mistake is assuming async replication is safe — a primary crash can lose recently committed transactions.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain GTID-based replication, how automated failover with Orchestrator or InnoDB Cluster works, and when Aurora or Spanner-style replication is preferable to self-managed binlog replication.

sections.title: How MySQL Replication Scales Reads and Enables Failover
sections.content:
MySQL replication lets one **primary** node stream all writes to one or more **replicas**.
- The primary records every committed change in a sequential binary log; each replica connects, downloads events, and applies them locally.
- This enables three production capabilities: **read scaling** by routing SELECTs to replicas, **high availability** by promoting a replica if the primary fails, and **zero-impact backups** taken from a replica.

The core trade-off is **replication lag**.
- Async replication commits on the primary before any replica acknowledges receipt, so a reader hitting a lagging replica immediately after a write may see the pre-write state.
- Lag is normally milliseconds but can spike to seconds during heavy writes, long transactions, or single-threaded SQL thread bottlenecks on the replica.

For a Spring Boot application the design question is always: which reads can tolerate stale data, which cannot, and how do we route accordingly?

sections.title: Binlog → I/O Thread → Relay Log → SQL Thread Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Primary
        clientWrite["Client Write"] --> engine["InnoDB Engine"]
        engine --> binlog["Binary Log (binlog)"]
    end
    subgraph Replica
        ioThread["I/O Thread"] --> relayLog["Relay Log"]
        relayLog --> sqlThread["SQL Thread / Workers"]
        sqlThread --> replicaData["Replica Tables"]
    end
    binlog -- "streamed events" --> ioThread
    readClient["Read Client"] --> replicaData
    writeClient["Write Client"] --> engine
```

sections.title: The Replication Pipeline in Detail
sections.content:
**Primary side — binlog generation**
- Every committed transaction writes events to the binary log in commit order
- `binlog_format = ROW` (recommended) records before/after row images; `STATEMENT` records raw SQL and breaks on non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `UUID()`
- `sync_binlog = 1` fsyncs the binlog on every commit — required for durability, costs write latency

**Replica side — two threads per channel**
- **I/O thread** opens a TCP connection to the primary, requests events from its last known position, and writes them to a local relay log on disk
- **SQL thread** reads from the relay log and executes events against the replica's tables; since MySQL 5.7 this can run as parallel workers (`slave_parallel_workers`)
- The replica tracks position by file+offset (legacy) or by GTID set (recommended)

```sql
-- Configure replica to follow a primary via GTID
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO
    SOURCE_HOST='primary.db.internal',
    SOURCE_USER='repl_user',
    SOURCE_PASSWORD='...',
    SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1;

START REPLICA;

-- Inspect replication health
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: replication lag in seconds
-- Replica_IO_Running / Replica_SQL_Running: must both be 'Yes'
-- Last_IO_Error / Last_SQL_Error: surface failures immediately
```

**Replication modes**
- **Async (default)**: primary commits before replicas acknowledge — lowest latency, highest data-loss risk on primary crash
- **Semi-sync** (`rpl_semi_sync_master_enabled = 1`): primary waits for at least one replica to acknowledge binlog receipt before returning to the client — bounds data loss
- **Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster**: synchronous multi-node consensus via a Paxos-derived protocol — no data loss, higher write latency

sections.title: Spring Boot Read/Write Routing with AbstractRoutingDataSource
GTID Replication, Automated Failover, and InnoDB Cluster
sections.content:
**GTID (Global Transaction Identifier) replication**
- Assigns every committed transaction a UUID:counter — e.g., `3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:23`
- Replicas track which GTIDs they have applied, so promoting any replica is a single command — other replicas auto-compute which GTIDs they still need
- Required for any setup with automated failover; enable with `gtid_mode=ON` + `enforce_gtid_consistency=ON`

**Automated failover with Orchestrator / MHA / Cloud**
- Health checker detects the primary is unreachable for N seconds
- Picks the replica with the most advanced applied GTID set as the new primary
- Waits for that replica to drain its relay log, promotes it, repoints other replicas
- Updates DNS or VIP so applications reach the new primary
- Typical RTO: 30–60 seconds; RPO depends on async vs semi-sync

**InnoDB Cluster / Group Replication**
- Three or more nodes form a consensus group; writes commit only after majority ack
- MySQL Router proxies connections, handling failover transparently
- Eliminates the async data-loss window at the cost of write latency

**Cloud-managed alternatives**
- AWS Aurora replaces binlog replication with a log-structured shared-storage layer; replica lag is typically under 100ms
- Google Spanner and CockroachDB extend the model to globally distributed strong consistency
- For new systems, evaluate whether managed services remove enough operational load to justify the premium

sections.title: Replication Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- Read-heavy workloads scale linearly by adding replicas
- Backups run on replicas without impacting primary throughput
- Analytical queries isolated from OLTP traffic
- Failover provides high availability with minutes-level RTO

**When it hurts:**
- Replication lag breaks read-your-writes — needs explicit routing to primary for recent writers
- Async replication allows data loss on primary crash — recent committed transactions not yet streamed are lost
- Single-threaded SQL thread becomes a bottleneck on write-heavy primaries; parallel workers require row-based replication
- Schema changes must be compatible across primary and replicas during rolling deploys

**Watch for:**
- `Seconds_Behind_Source` spikes during bulk DML or long transactions
- Replica disk full from relay log accumulation after SQL thread errors
- Statement-based replication bugs with `NOW()`, `RAND()`, `AUTO_INCREMENT` in mixed environments
- Replication breaks silently when `binlog_format` differs between primary and replica

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Async replication allows data loss on primary crash** — the primary commits and acknowledges before any replica confirms receipt; semi-sync replication eliminates this window at the cost of write latency
- **Replication lag breaks read-your-writes** — a user reads from a lagging replica immediately after writing and sees the old value; route reads to the primary for a short post-write window
- **Row-based replication (binlog_format=ROW) is safer than statement-based** — it replicates exact row changes; statement-based breaks for non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `RAND()`
- **`SHOW REPLICA STATUS` is the first monitoring check** — `Seconds_Behind_Source`, `Replica_IO_Running`, `Replica_SQL_Running`, and `Last_SQL_Error` surface every common failure mode
- **GTID-based replication simplifies failover** — Global Transaction IDs make promoting any replica a single command instead of computing binlog coordinates by hand

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL primary-replica replication is the standard way to scale reads — the primary handles all writes and streams changes to replicas via the binary log.

**How it works**
- Every write on the primary is recorded in the binary log in commit order — each replica runs an I/O thread that pulls binlog events into a local relay log, and an SQL thread that replays those events
- Replication is asynchronous by default, which means there's always some lag — how much depends on replica hardware and primary write rate

**Async vs semi-sync vs Group Replication**
- Async: primary acknowledges commit before any replica confirms — lowest latency, but a primary crash can lose recently committed transactions
- Semi-sync: primary waits for at least one replica to ack binlog receipt — bounds data loss at the cost of a small latency bump
- Group Replication: synchronous multi-node consensus — no data loss, higher write latency; used in InnoDB Cluster

**Read routing in Spring Boot**
- Configure separate DataSource beans for primary and replica, wire them into an `AbstractRoutingDataSource` that picks based on `@Transactional(readOnly=true)`
- For read-your-writes, remember the user just wrote and route their next reads to the primary for a short window — otherwise they hit a lagging replica and see stale data

Row-based replication is the production default — it replicates exact row changes and avoids the determinism bugs that plague statement-based replication.

questions.question: How does PostgreSQL streaming replication work, and when do you use logical replication instead?
questions.title: PostgreSQL Streaming vs Logical Replication
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL offers two replication families. **Streaming (physical) replication** ships **WAL** records from the primary to standbys byte-for-byte — the standby is an exact block-level copy, great for HA and read scaling but bound to the same major version and cluster-wide. **Logical replication** decodes WAL into logical row changes per publication and applies them on the subscriber, enabling cross-version upgrades, selective table replication, and cross-database data movement. Sync modes range from async (default) to `synchronous_commit=remote_apply` for zero data loss.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish physical (WAL-level) from logical (row-level) replication, pick the right mode for HA vs migration vs CDC, and configure replication slots, synchronous commit, and publications correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using streaming replication for zero-downtime major-version upgrades — it cannot cross major versions. Another is forgetting to drop orphaned replication slots, which causes the primary's WAL to grow until disk fills.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain replication slots and why they are required for reliable standbys, how `pg_stat_replication` diagnoses lag, and how logical replication underpins Debezium-based CDC pipelines.

sections.title: Two Replication Models, Two Different Problems
sections.content:
PostgreSQL ships with two complementary replication systems built on top of the **write-ahead log (WAL)**. Every modification — DML, DDL, index updates, vacuum work — is recorded to WAL before the data page is marked dirty; replication reuses this log.

**Streaming (physical) replication** transports raw WAL bytes to standby servers, which apply them block-for-block.
- The standby is a physical twin of the primary, suitable for **hot standby reads** and **fast failover**.
- It cannot cross major versions, cannot selectively replicate a subset of tables, and cannot be written to while acting as standby.

**Logical replication** decodes WAL into a logical change stream (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE per table) and ships that stream to subscribers, which apply the changes through normal SQL. This enables **major-version upgrades with minimal downtime**, **partial replication** (specific tables or schemas), and **CDC pipelines** via tools like Debezium.

Knowing which to use for a given problem is the senior-level signal interviewers probe for.

sections.title: Physical vs Logical Replication
sections.content:
A short way to see the choice: physical is for HA and read scaling within a cluster; logical is for moving data across versions, databases, or systems.

| Dimension | Streaming (Physical) | Logical |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of replication | Raw WAL bytes | Decoded row changes per table |
| Cross major versions | No | Yes (PG 10+) |
| Selective tables | No | Yes via publications |
| Writes on replica | No (read-only) | Yes (each side independent) |
| DDL replication | Automatic | Not replicated (manual) |
| Typical use | HA, read replicas, PITR base | Upgrades, CDC, multi-master patterns |
| Tooling | `pg_basebackup`, replication slot | `CREATE PUBLICATION/SUBSCRIPTION`, Debezium |

sections.title: Streaming Replication Topology
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Primary
        client["Client Writes"] --> wal["WAL Writer"]
        wal --> walFiles["pg_wal segments"]
        walFiles --> slot["Replication Slot"]
    end
    subgraph StandbyA["Hot Standby A (sync)"]
        walReceiverA["walreceiver"] --> applyA["startup/recovery"]
        applyA --> standbyDataA["Standby Heap & Indexes"]
    end
    subgraph StandbyB["Hot Standby B (async)"]
        walReceiverB["walreceiver"] --> applyB["startup/recovery"]
        applyB --> standbyDataB["Standby Heap & Indexes"]
    end
    slot --> walReceiverA
    slot --> walReceiverB
    readerA["Read-only Query"] --> standbyDataA
    readerB["Read-only Query"] --> standbyDataB
```

sections.title: Configuring Streaming Replication with Replication Slots
sections.content:
**Primary setup**
- Set `wal_level = replica`, `max_wal_senders = 10`, `max_replication_slots = 10` in `postgresql.conf`
- Allow replication connections in `pg_hba.conf`: `host replication replicator 10.0.0.0/8 scram-sha-256`
- Create a role for replication: `CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD '...';`
- Create a **replication slot** so the primary retains WAL until the standby consumes it

```sql
-- On the primary
SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('standby_a');
```

**Standby setup**
- Take a base backup that copies the data directory and WAL: `pg_basebackup -h primary -D /var/lib/pgsql/17/data -U replicator -X stream -S standby_a -R`
- The `-R` flag writes `standby.signal` and adds `primary_conninfo` to `postgresql.auto.conf`
- Start the standby — it connects, streams WAL, and enters hot-standby read-only mode

**Monitoring**
```sql
-- On the primary
SELECT client_addr, state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) AS apply_lag_bytes
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- On the standby
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(),
       now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay;
```

**The replication-slot hazard**
- Slots guarantee the primary keeps WAL until the standby replays it
- If a standby is removed without dropping its slot, WAL accumulates until `pg_wal` fills the disk and the primary stops accepting writes
- Always `SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('standby_a');` when retiring a standby

sections.title: Logical Replication and CDC Pipelines
sections.content:
**Publication/Subscription model**
- The publisher declares which tables to publish
- Each subscriber has an independent copy and can write to other tables or receive publications from multiple publishers

```sql
-- On the publisher (source)
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = 'logical';
-- restart
CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE orders, order_items, customers;

-- On the subscriber (target)
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION app_sub
    CONNECTION 'host=publisher.db user=replicator password=... dbname=app'
    PUBLICATION app_pub;
```

**Use cases**
- **Zero-downtime major upgrades**: set up a PG 17 subscriber reading from a PG 14 publisher, let it catch up, switch the application at a quiet moment
- **Selective replication**: replicate only customer-facing tables to a read-only analytics node
- **Cross-region read models**: maintain a denormalized copy per region without full cluster replication
- **CDC via Debezium**: Debezium attaches as a logical-replication consumer using the `pgoutput` plugin, publishes row changes to Kafka, and feeds downstream search indexes, caches, and warehouses

**Gotchas**
- DDL is not replicated — run schema migrations on both sides (Flyway/Liquibase helps)
- Primary keys are required on replicated tables (or `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, which is expensive)
- Large initial copies can stall WAL retention — monitor `pg_replication_slots.wal_status`
- Sequences are not advanced on the subscriber; resync at cutover

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content:
**When streaming replication helps:**
- Same-version HA with fast failover via Patroni or repmgr
- Read scaling for analytics and reports that tolerate sub-second lag
- Physical backups via `pg_basebackup` plus WAL archive for PITR

**When streaming replication hurts:**
- Cannot upgrade PostgreSQL major versions without downtime
- Cannot replicate a subset of tables or a single database only
- Cannot accept writes on the standby

**When logical replication helps:**
- Near-zero-downtime major-version upgrades
- CDC pipelines into Kafka, Elasticsearch, Snowflake via Debezium
- Per-region read models, multi-tenant data distribution

**Watch for:**
- Orphaned replication slots filling `pg_wal` and halting writes
- `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` destroying write latency if the sync standby is geographically far
- DDL drift between publisher and subscriber breaking logical replication silently

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Physical replication is block-level, logical is row-level** — physical standbys are exact copies; logical subscribers apply decoded INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events and can diverge
- **Replication slots prevent WAL loss but risk disk fill** — they guarantee the primary keeps WAL until the replica consumes it; always drop slots when retiring standbys
- **`synchronous_commit` controls the durability guarantee** — `off` is fire-and-forget, `on` fsyncs locally, `remote_write` and `remote_apply` wait on a sync standby
- **Logical replication is the standard upgrade path** — spin up a new-version subscriber, catch up, switch the application; downtime is measured in seconds
- **Debezium uses `pgoutput` as a logical consumer** — it reads the same change stream that logical replication uses and publishes events to Kafka for CDC pipelines

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PostgreSQL has two replication systems and choosing the right one is usually half the interview answer.

**Streaming replication — for HA and read scaling**
- Ships raw WAL bytes from the primary to standbys that replay them block-for-block; the standby is an identical copy and can serve read-only queries
- Configure `wal_level=replica`, create a replication slot so the primary keeps WAL until the standby consumes it, and take a base backup with `pg_basebackup -R` to bootstrap the standby
- Monitor with `pg_stat_replication` — the LSN diff between `sent_lsn` and `replay_lsn` is your lag metric

**Logical replication — for upgrades and partial copies**
- Decodes WAL into row-level change events and ships them per publication; subscribers apply through regular SQL, so cross-version and cross-database replication work
- Used for zero-downtime major-version upgrades, selective replication of a few tables, and CDC into Kafka via Debezium's `pgoutput` plugin
- Requires primary keys on replicated tables and manual DDL propagation — run Flyway on both sides

**Pitfalls worth mentioning**
- Orphaned replication slots fill `pg_wal` and bring down the primary — always drop slots when retiring standbys
- Synchronous commit modes trade durability for write latency; pick based on how far the sync standby is geographically

In practice: streaming for HA, logical for anything that crosses a boundary — version, database, or system.
